name: Battle of Plataea
info: In August 479 BCE a Spartan-led Greek alliance defeated the Achaemenid army of Mardonius near Plataea in Boeotia, killing Mardonius and trapping much of his army in its camp, which ended the second Persian invasion of Greece.

facts.date: August 479 BCE; Paul A. Rahe and Theodore Cuyler Young Jr. estimate 27 August, Rahe allowing the 27th or 28th
facts.place: Near the city of Plataea in Boeotia, central Greece, on and around the Asopos river; the Persian camp stood on its north bank
facts.sides: The Hellenic alliance led by Sparta, with Athens, Corinth, Tegea, Megara and other city-states, under the Spartan regent Pausanias, with 78,000 soldiers by Konecny's estimate; an Achaemenid army under Mardonius, allied with Boeotia, Thessaly and Macedon, with 70,000 by Lazenby's estimate and 120,000 by Connolly's
facts.outcome: The Greeks routed the Persian infantry and killed Mardonius, then stormed the Persian camp. The second Persian invasion of Greece ended.

t: Figures for both armies rest on estimates. Herodotus gives the Spartan contribution as 45,000 men, and modern estimates of the Persian army run from 40,000 to 120,000, mostly from the size of its camp.
The Greek retreat on the night before the battle went wrong, and Mardonius, thinking the Greeks were in full retreat, ordered a pursuit that brought on the fighting.
Herodotus gives 652 Greek dead, Plutarch 1,360 and Diodorus 10,000, and says only 3,000 Persians survived the fighting at the camp.
dyk: Herodotus says the Spartans sent 45,000 men, of whom 5,000 were Spartiates and 35,000 helots, seven helots for each Spartiate, and one tenth of the Persian loot went to the regent Pausanias, not to the state of Sparta.
ev: A small Allied army under Leonidas I holds Thermopylae for three days, and the Allied fleet then defeats the Persian navy at Salamis
Xerxes retreats to Sardis with a minor portion of his army and leaves Mardonius in charge of his troops
The Persians march south again and Athens is evacuated a second time, and the Spartans march out only after the Athenians threaten to accept Persian terms
The Greeks cross Mount Cithaeron and take positions opposite the Persian camp, and cavalry fighting leaves the Persian commander Masistius dead
Persian cavalry cuts the Greek supply route and blocks the Gargaphian spring, and the Greeks retreat by night
Mardonius pursues the retreating Greeks and is killed, and the Greeks storm the Persian camp
The Greeks besiege Thebes after ten days and execute most of the pro-Persian leaders they find

sections.background:
Xerxes I, after his accession in 486 BCE, prepared an invasion of Greece, including two pontoon bridges across the Hellespont. A congress of city states met, probably at Corinth, in 481 BCE and formed a confederate alliance generally called the Allies. In August 480 BCE a small Allied army under the Spartan king Leonidas I blocked the pass of Thermopylae for three days before the Persians outflanked it by a little-known mountain path. The Persians then burned and sacked Plataea and Thespiae, which had not surrendered, and took the evacuated city of Athens. The naval Battle of Salamis ended in an Allied victory, and Xerxes retreated to Sardis with a minor portion of his army.

Xerxes left Mardonius in charge of his troops, and Mardonius spent the winter in Thessaly. He tried to win over the Athenians through Alexander I of Macedon, and when they refused the Persians marched south again and Athens was again evacuated. Mardonius repeated his offer of peace to the Athenian refugees on Salamis. Athens sent emissaries to Sparta demanding help and threatened to accept the Persian terms if it was not given. According to Herodotus the Spartans were celebrating the festival of Hyacinthus and delayed ten days, until persuaded of the danger to all Greece. When the Athenian envoys delivered their ultimatum to the ephors, they were told that the army had already left: the 5,000 Spartiates were at Oresthasium.
sections.forces:
According to Herodotus the Spartans sent 45,000 men: 5,000 Spartiates, 5,000 other Lacedaemonian hoplites (perioeci) and 35,000 helots. Pausanias, regent for his cousin Pleistarchus, commanded the Spartans and chose Euryanax as his deputy, and the Athenians were under Aristides. Ian Macgregor-Morris argues that the Spartiates were three fifths of Sparta's troops, while Hans van Wees argues they were all the citizens then fit to serve. Nicholas Sekunda argues that Herodotus inflated the allied army to 110,000 by assuming a lightly armed attendant for each hoplite; Andreas Konecny estimates 78,000 Greek soldiers. Argos, Mantinea and Elis sent no troops.

The Persians built a fortified camp of about 1.9 square kilometres on the north bank of the Asopos. John Francis Lazenby, comparing its size with Roman camps, calculates 70,000 men including 10,000 cavalry, and Peter Connolly 120,000, and most estimates lie in this range. Hans Delbrück took 75,000 as the upper limit including supply personnel and other non-combatants, and put the army including allied Greeks at 40,000. Konecny estimates 44,000 to 66,000 infantry and 5,000 to 7,000 cavalry.

In Herodotus's arrangement the Persians faced the 11,500 Lacedaemonian and Tegean hoplites, the Medes, Bactrians, Indians and Sacae stood in the centre, and the Boeotians, Locrians, Malians, Thessalians and Phocians faced 11,600 Athenians, Plataeans and Megarians. Thorax of Larissa and his brothers were with Mardonius.
sections.course:
The Greeks took positions on high ground on Mount Cithaeron, about 4 kilometres across the Asopos from the Persian camp. Mardonius began hit-and-run cavalry attacks. When cavalry under Masistius attacked the Megarians, 300 Athenians under Olympiodoros and their archers took their place, and Masistius was killed after an archer hit his horse. The Greeks moved to a position nearer the Asopos. The armies then stayed in place for eight days; Herodotus says both sides had received bad omens from their seers. Mardonius sent cavalry against a Greek supply convoy and blocked the Gargaphian spring, the Greeks' only source of water.

After 12 days at the second position the Greeks decided to retreat by night to a place called the island, in front of Plataea. The retreat went awry. The centre advanced 1.8 kilometres past the island to the Temple of Hera, and the Spartans and Tegeans had not moved by daybreak because the Spartan commander Amompharetus refused to retreat, thinking it cowardly. The Athenians and Plataeans were blocked by the scattered centre.

Mardonius hurried with his left wing, about 5 kilometres, after Pausanias's line. Persian archers fired from behind a shield wall and Greek soldiers began to fall. Herodotus says Pausanias would not advance without good omens; the Tegeans ran at the Persian lines and Pausanias then ordered the Spartans to charge. Roel Konijnendijk argues that a soldier named Aeimnestus killed Mardonius with a thrown stone. The Persian guards broke, the rest followed, and the Athenians fought the Thebans, who eventually retreated.
sections.aftermath:
The Greeks chased the Persians to their camp. The Spartans arrived first and waited for the Athenians, who knew how to scale walls, and the Tegeans were the first to breach them. Herodotus estimates that only 3,000 Persians survived the fighting at the camp; Konecny argues that 3,000 may be the prisoners taken, while others fled. Artabazos led 40,000 men away to Phocis and reached the Hellespont, losing many soldiers to Thracian attacks, weariness and hunger. Herodotus says the Battle of Mycale was fought on the same day.

The Spartan dead were buried in three graves, the helots in the third. Pausanias refused Lampon of Aegina's proposal to desecrate Mardonius's corpse in revenge for the mutilation of Leonidas. One tenth of the Persian loot went to Pausanias and not to Sparta, which concerned the Spartans.

After ten days the Greeks besieged Thebes. The leading pro-Persian politician, Attaginus, escaped and his sons were pardoned, but the other medisers were executed without trial. According to Vitruvius, Caryae, which had medized, was captured, its men executed and its women enslaved. After Mycale the Athenians besieged Sestos, and the Persian general Artayctes was crucified there and his son stoned to death by Xanthippus.
sections.sources:
Herodotus gives the main account. Ctesias, a Greek physician at the court of Artaxerxes II, wrote one drawn largely from Persian sources. Diodorus Siculus based his on Ephorus, and Plutarch cited Idomeneus of Lampsacus and Simonides. Herodotus says the Corinthians did not follow Pausanias's orders and took no part, while Simonides says they played a major part. Ray Nyland argues that the Greeks Herodotus consulted had not fought in the battle, while the pro-Persian Greeks and Persians he consulted very probably had, and that he did not cite them because they were not considered reliable.

Casualty figures are uncertain. The Greek dead are 652 in Herodotus, 1,360 in Plutarch and 10,000 in Diodorus. Herodotus probably could not count the Spartan perioeci. His 52 Athenian dead may be only the tribe Aiantis's memorial, as Cleidemus suggested, and Michael Flower and John Marincola argue he gave the Greek losses only for the final day.

Historians dispute the shape of the battle. Konijnendijk and Paul Bardunias argue that the picture of a phalanx battle is contrary to the evidence, and that the Greeks formed a defensive line, sent out small groups to provoke the Persians and then pushed. Robert Gaebel argues that the cavalry covering the Persian retreat were Boeotian, led by Asopodoros. Rahe and Young give the date as 27 August; Rahe also allows the 28th.
sections.legacy:
The Serpent Column, a bronze of intertwined snakes made from melted-down Persian armour, was erected at Delphi and listed the 31 Greek city-states that took part. Most of it survives in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, in present-day Istanbul. Pausanias sacrificed to Zeus Eleutherios in the agora of Plataea, where a marble altar was built, and the Athenians built the Stoa of Zeus in their agora. The Eleutheria, a festival of Zeus Eleutherios, included a race of 3 kilometres run in armour with a shield.

Simonides of Ceos wrote an encomium and an elegy on the battle. Marcello Lupi contends that the Spartans commissioned them, possibly through Pausanias, since they glorify both, and that in Spartan propaganda the victory avenged Thermopylae. Christel Müller argues that Plataea became a place of memory. Herodotus says some states built cenotaphs there; Müller argues they did so out of shame at not having taken part, while Lazenby argues these states had suffered casualties but could not recover their dead or had buried them in a collective grave.

George Cawkwell argues that the main lesson was the superiority of the hoplite over Persian light infantry, that Persia afterwards relied on Greek mercenaries, and that Greece was lost to Persia through Plataea rather than Salamis. Plutarch says Alexander the Great recognised that Plataea had paved the way for his conquest. Spoils funded buildings such as the Athenian Treasury at Delphi, and Caroline Vout argues that the victories at Plataea and Mycale heralded the Greek incorporation of Persian culture.

summary: At Plataea in August 479 BCE the Spartan-led Greek alliance defeated Mardonius's Achaemenid army, and Mardonius died in the fighting. Estimates of the armies and the dead vary widely, and the battle ended the second Persian invasion of Greece, together with the naval defeat at Mycale.

William Shepherd, Plataea 479 BC: The Most Glorious Victory Ever Seen (Osprey Publishing, 2012)
Paul Cartledge, After Thermopylae: The Oath of Plataea and the End of the Graeco-Persian Wars (Oxford University Press, 2013)
John Francis Lazenby, The Defence of Greece, 490-479 B.C. (Aris & Phillips, 1993)

notes: Date: the article gives only 'August 479 BC' in its lead; Rahe and Young estimate 27 August, Rahe also the 28th. Span uses 'August 479 BCE'.

Strengths: Herodotus's Greek total is not stated in the article except as Sekunda's account of an inflated 110,000; the 45,000 is the Spartan contribution only. Persian figures are modern estimates from camp size (Lazenby 70,000, Connolly 120,000, Delbruck 40,000 or 75,000 upper limit, Konecny 44,000-66,000 infantry). Konecny's 78,000 for the Greeks is given only in the logistics section.

The article contradicts itself or is thin in places: Konecny says only 10,000 helots fought while Hunt, Konijnendijk and Bardunias say all were deployed; I left the helots' role out of the battle text. The article says both that the Athenians were engaged by the Thebans and that Persians were not in formation; I kept only what is clearly stated.

The article says Mardonius was killed by Aeimnestus under Konijnendijk's account only; I attributed it. Herodotus's omens explanation for the eight-day stalemate is given with Konecny's alternative (both waiting for the other to attack) left out for length.

Left out for length: Konecny's and Sekunda's supply and water calculations, Young's logistics figures, the individual anecdotes (Aristodemus, Callicrates), de Jong's and Millender's readings of the spoils and the helots selling gold to the Aeginetans, Konijnendijk's analysis of cavalry and missile troops, Lazenby's comparison with Marathon.

The info line says 'trapping much of his army in its camp' following the article's lead ('a large portion of the Persian army was trapped in its camp and killed'); the aftermath keeps Herodotus's figure of 3,000 survivors and Konecny's doubt.
'Decisive': the lead says the destruction of the army and Mycale decisively ended the invasion; I wrote that the battle ended the invasion without the adverb.
The ev entry dated 'Summer 479 BCE' rests on Konecny's estimate for the crossing of Cithaeron (late July to mid August); Masistius's death follows soon after in the article without a date.
